description: Width tiers for Mathematics Year 10 — ACARA v9. All 21 descriptors across Algebra, Measurement, Number, Probability, Space and Statistics strands.
subject: Mathematics

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest construction that honestly satisfies the descriptor's command term. Set by the verb — 'solve' requires a solution, 'recognise' requires identification with explanation, 'construct' requires a built artefact. Not what is easy or common; what the descriptor actually demands at minimum.
width_notes.typical_width: The full scope of the descriptor as ACARA intended it, grounded in the most common elaboration cases. Reflects sound standard practice — what a class that has engaged with the descriptor fully would have done.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add phenomena, contexts or task types — not harder versions of the same context. First Nations elaborations are included as default wider directions where ACARA elaborations indicate them.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations are preserved verbatim as source data. They are examples of how the descriptor might be addressed, not a required sequence or checklist.

AC9M10A01.minimum_width: Expand and factorise simple quadratic expressions using the distributive property; apply exponent laws (products, quotients, powers) to simplify algebraic expressions with positive integral exponents.
AC9M10A01.typical_width: Expand and factorise a range of quadratic expressions including difference of two squares, perfect squares, and non-monic forms; apply exponent laws including negative integral exponents to simplify algebraic expressions and solve equations algebraically; explain the relationship between factorisation and expansion including completed square form.
wider: Investigate how the completed square form reveals properties of quadratic functions (vertex form) and connect to graphical representations
Apply exponent laws in contexts that cross into other strands — e.g. simplifying expressions arising from measurement or probability models
Explore historical and cultural contexts in which symbolic algebra was developed, including contributions from Islamic mathematicians and connections to First Nations counting and patterning systems
elaborations: explaining the relationship between factorisation and expansion, including the completed square form for quadratic expressions
applying knowledge of exponent laws to algebraic terms and using both positive and negative integral exponents to simplifying algebraic expressions and solve equations algebraically

AC9M10A02.minimum_width: Solve a pair of simultaneous linear equations in 2 variables algebraically or graphically; interpret the solution in terms of a given context.
AC9M10A02.typical_width: Solve linear inequalities and simultaneous linear equations in 2 variables using algebraic and graphical methods; graph solution regions for inequalities in the Cartesian plane; verify solutions using test points; communicate solutions using appropriate context language (break-even, budget constraints); identify integer solutions for practical constraints.
wider: Investigate situations with three or more constraints forming a feasible region and discuss optimal solutions in linear programming contexts
Explore how simultaneous equations model supply and demand, cost-benefit, or resource allocation in authentic economic or environmental contexts
Investigate the strategies inherent in First Nations Australian children's instructive games (e.g. Weme from the Warlpiri Peoples) and their connection to solving simultaneous linear equations
elaborations: investigating situations involving linear equations in context, such as multiple quotes for a job, or profit and loss; solving the equations graphically, giving solutions in everyday language
describing the solution of simultaneous equations within the context of the situation
graphing regions corresponding to inequalities in the Cartesian plane and verifying using a test point
identifying all the combinations of activities as integer solutions for a budget; expressing algebraically as an inequality
testing when a circle of a specified radius has a corresponding area greater than a given value, or whether a point satisfies an inequality

investigating the strategies inherent in First Nations Australian children's instructive games (e.g. Weme from the Warlpiri Peoples) and their connection to strategies to solve simultaneous linear equations in 2 variables

AC9M10A03.minimum_width: Recognise that a constant ratio between consecutive dependent variable values in a table indicates an exponential relation; sketch or interpret the graph of a simple exponential function and connect it to its equation.
AC9M10A03.typical_width: Recognise exponential relations from tables of values (constant ratio), equations and graphs; connect algebraic and graphical representations using digital tools; solve simple exponential equations; investigate exponential growth and decay in at least two applied contexts.
wider: Formulate and solve exponential equations modelling population competition between feral and native animals on Country/Place, evaluating the model's assumptions
Investigate how exponential functions underpin compound interest, radioactive decay, and biological population models — comparing the same mathematical structure across different phenomena
Explore how digital tools with symbolic manipulation reveal parameter effects on exponential graphs, making and testing conjectures about transformations
elaborations: recognising that in a table of values, if the ratio between consecutive values of the dependent variable is constant, then it is an exponential relation
investigating the links between algebraic and graphical representations of exponential functions using graphing software
using digital tools with symbolic manipulation functionality to systematically explore exponential relations

investigating First Nations Australian Ranger groups' and other groups' programs that attempt to eradicate feral animals for survival of native animals on Country/Place, exploring the competition between feral and native animals and their impact on natural resources by formulating exponential equations for population growth

AC9M10A04.minimum_width: Select and apply one of linear, quadratic or exponential models to a given growth or decay situation; interpret the solution in terms of the context and state key assumptions.
AC9M10A04.typical_width: Formulate problems involving growth and decay by selecting appropriate models (linear, quadratic or exponential) using first differences, second differences or constant ratio to justify model choice; determine doubling time or half-life for exponential models; model compound interest using authentic data; interpret and evaluate solutions in context; report assumptions and methods.
wider: Investigate how exponential equations are used in carbon dating to estimate the age of First Nations Australians' artefacts, discussing measurement assumptions and uncertainty
Model and critique population growth situations for native animals on Country/Place using exponential equations, evaluating the real-world applicability of the model
Compare linear, quadratic and exponential models fitted to the same data set and evaluate which best represents the situation, discussing limitations of each
elaborations: modelling situations and choosing between linear, quadratic and exponential models by representing relationships in a table of values and recognising constant first differences, constant second differences, and constant ratio
modelling situations involving exponential growth and decay; determining doubling time and half-life
modelling situations involving compound interest using authentic data and interest rates
modelling and investigating how exponential equations are used in carbon dating to estimate the age of First Nations Australians' artefacts or material culture
modelling and formulating situations involving population growth of native animals on Country/Place with varying reproductive behaviour, using exponential equations and critiquing their applicability

AC9M10A05.minimum_width: Use a digital graphing tool to explore at least two types of functions or relations; make and test at least one conjecture about a pattern observed (e.g. effect of a parameter on a graph).
AC9M10A05.typical_width: Use digital tools to experiment with linear, quadratic, exponential and circular functions/relations; apply zoom and bisection methods to locate intersection points and axis intercepts; identify where functions are positive or negative; apply transformations to a circle; make, test and generalise conjectures about emerging patterns across function families.
wider: Investigate how functions and relations serve as the mathematical underpinning of machine learning — how data is transformed, models defined and optimisation performed
Apply a bisection algorithm to systematically narrow intervals for roots of polynomial functions, connecting the numerical method to graphical behaviour
Explore how parameter variation in exponential or quadratic functions connects to real-world modelling decisions (e.g. growth rate, vertex position) and generalise rules about transformations
elaborations: applying the graphing zoom functionality and systematically refining intervals to identify approximate location of points of intersection
applying a bisection algorithm to determine the approximate location of horizontal axis intercepts of a quadratic
applying transformations to the graph of x² + y² = 1
identifying coordinates of intersection points of linear with quadratic or circular functions
identifying intervals where a given quadratic function is positive or negative
using a table of values to determine when an exponential growth or decay function exceeds or falls below a given value
investigating how functions and relations serve as the mathematical underpinnings of machine learning

AC9M10M01.minimum_width: Calculate the surface area and volume of a composite solid formed from two familiar right prisms or cylinders by considering its component parts.
AC9M10M01.typical_width: Determine surface area and volume of composite solids formed from combinations of right prisms, cylinders and other familiar 3D shapes; estimate surface area and volume in practical contexts; use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving composite objects (e.g. rainwater storage, capacity planning), stating assumptions and interpreting results.
wider: Design and evaluate optimal composite container shapes for a given volume constraint (e.g. rainwater tank fitting under a deck), modelling and comparing multiple configurations
Investigate how surface area to volume ratio affects real-world phenomena (heat loss, cell size, packaging efficiency) using composite object models
Explore how traditional First Nations architectural or material culture structures use composite forms and investigate their spatial properties
elaborations: determining the volumes and surface areas of composite solids formed from right prisms and cylinders
estimating the surface area and volume of composite objects in practical contexts
using mathematical modelling to solve problems involving surface area and volume (e.g. rainwater collection, optimal storage dimensions, event supply planning)

AC9M10M02.minimum_width: Read and interpret a graph or chart that uses a logarithmic scale; explain why a logarithmic scale is appropriate for the context (e.g. range of values, rate of change).
AC9M10M02.typical_width: Interpret and use logarithmic scales across multiple applied contexts (Richter, decibel, pH, exponential growth); identify when a logarithmic scale is more appropriate than a linear scale; compare representations of the same data on linear and logarithmic axes; discuss the meaning of equal intervals on a log scale (order of magnitude).
wider: Investigate how logarithmic scaling is used in dating methods at geological sites significant to First Peoples of Australia, including the Madjedbebe dig — examining scientific notation, measurement accuracy, and the social implications of the findings
Explore how machine learning algorithms use logarithmic scaling to compress large value ranges and investigate what this means for how data is processed
Compare how the same phenomenon (e.g. earthquake magnitude, sound intensity) appears on linear vs logarithmic axes and explain why the logarithmic representation is more informative
elaborations: understanding that the logarithmic scale is calibrated in terms of order of magnitude
identifying and interpreting data representations that use logarithmic scales and discussing when appropriate vs not appropriate
investigating and interpreting logarithmic scales in real-world contexts (Richter, decibel, sensitivity scales, growth in investments, spread of micro-organisms)
investigating how logarithmic scaling can be used in machine learning algorithms to compress large values
investigating dating methods of geological sites including the Madjedbebe dig using logarithmic scales and measurement accuracy

AC9M10M03.minimum_width: Apply Pythagoras' theorem and at least one trigonometric ratio to solve a practical right-angled triangle problem involving an angle of elevation or depression.
AC9M10M03.typical_width: Apply Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry (sin, cos, tan) to solve multi-step practical problems including bearings, angles of elevation and depression, and surveying contexts; decompose 3D problems into 2D; use clinometers or digital tools to measure and calculate; model and solve problems in at least three different practical contexts.
wider: Explore navigation, design of technologies or surveying methods used by First Nations Australians, investigating the geometric and spatial reasoning involved and how these connect to trigonometric principles
Investigate how autonomous vehicles use Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry to calculate distance and navigate spaces, including practical implications of sensor accuracy
Design and solve a complex multi-step problem (e.g. crime scene reconstruction, orienteering course design) that requires decomposing 3D spatial relationships into multiple 2D trigonometric problems
elaborations: applying right-angled trigonometry to solve navigation problems involving bearings
applying Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry to surveying and design, decomposing 3D problems into 2D
using a clinometer to measure angles of inclination and applying trigonometry to determine building heights
applying Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry with dynamic geometric software to model elevation and depression situations
investigating how autonomous vehicles use Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry to calculate distance and navigate
exploring navigation and surveying by First Nations Australians and connections to trigonometry

AC9M10M04.minimum_width: Identify at least one source of measurement error in a practical context and describe how it affects the accuracy of a result.
AC9M10M04.typical_width: Identify and describe sources of measurement error across multiple practical contexts (research, financial, engineering); explain how compounding errors accumulate across repeated calculations; analyse instruments and methods for measuring; discuss how measurement errors can produce biased findings.
wider: Investigate scientific measuring techniques applied to First Peoples of Australia — including dating methods and genetic sequencing — and discuss the social impact of measurement errors in these contexts
Analyse measurement errors in the perception and control systems of autonomous vehicles, including sensor limitations and their safety implications
Compare how truncation vs rounding errors propagate differently through financial calculations at scale (e.g. large customer populations) and quantify the cumulative effect
elaborations: describing settings where measurement errors may impact research results and cause biased findings
analysing instruments and methods for measuring in investigations and modelling activities
determining the impact of compounding errors on financial calculations (e.g. truncation for large customer populations)
investigating the impact of measurement errors in perception and control systems of autonomous vehicles
investigating scientific measuring techniques including dating methods and genetic sequencing applied to First Peoples of Australia and the social impact of measurement errors

AC9M10M05.minimum_width: Use proportion and scaling to solve a practical problem involving a scale drawing or model; identify the scale factor and convert between model and actual measurements.
AC9M10M05.typical_width: Use mathematical modelling to solve practical proportion and scaling problems in at least two contexts (architectural plans, prototypes, 3D printing); determine scale factors from measurements; evaluate the suitability of models; report assumptions and methods; investigate compliance with real-world standards or codes.
wider: Investigate how AI image generators use proportion and scaling techniques such as aspect ratio preservation to maintain realistic visual relationships, and critically evaluate the outputs
Design a scaled physical or digital model of a real object (e.g. architectural structure, vehicle), documenting all scaling decisions and comparing model dimensions to actual specifications
Analyse compliance with Australian building codes for a specific design (e.g. staircase gradient, escalator dimensions) using proportion and mathematical modelling
elaborations: using plans and elevation drawings to investigate building design changes, employing appropriate scales
analysing and applying scale and ratios in production prototypes and 3D printing
estimating the scale of an object by measuring a linear dimension and using typical dimensions
investigating compliance with building codes in design and construction (e.g. escalators)
investigating how AI image generators use proportion and scaling techniques to preserve aspect ratios

AC9M10N01.minimum_width: Show, using at least one worked example, that truncating or rounding a real number before repeated calculation produces a different result than using the exact representation; describe the nature of the difference.
AC9M10N01.typical_width: Compare and contrast the effect of truncation vs rounding on results in multiple repeated-calculation contexts (compound shapes, surface area/volume, repeated interest); explain when approximation error is negligible and when it is significant; use exact representations (surds, fractions) where appropriate and compare results.
wider: Investigate how floating-point representation in computers introduces approximation error and compare this to the mathematical concept of exact vs approximate representation
Explore contexts where cumulative approximation errors have real consequences (e.g. financial rounding at scale, navigation drift) and quantify the accumulated error

Limited width note: this descriptor has genuinely thin context breadth — the core concept (approximation error in repeated calculation) does not vary substantially across phenomena at Y10. The wider directions above go slightly further conceptually rather than truly broadening context.
elaborations: comparing and contrasting the effect of truncation or rounding on the final result of calculations when using approximations rather than exact representations
investigating the impact of approximation on multiple calculations in contexts involving compound shapes, surface area/volume of compound objects, and repeated simple interest calculations
AC9M10N01.width_notes: Thin width descriptor — the concept of approximation error in repeated calculation does not vary meaningfully across phenomena at this year band. Typical width covers the elaboration scope fully. Wider directions extend conceptually (computer arithmetic, real-world consequence) rather than adding genuinely new phenomena.

AC9M10P01.minimum_width: Use the language of conditional probability ('given', 'if...then', 'knowing that') correctly in at least one context; use a two-way table or Venn diagram to calculate a simple conditional probability.
AC9M10P01.typical_width: Use conditional probability language correctly across multiple contexts; use two-way tables, Venn diagrams, arrays and tree diagrams to represent and calculate probabilities of dependent and independent events; identify and explain common language errors in interpreting conditional statements.
wider: Investigate how conditional probability underpins natural language processing tasks (text generation, translation, recommendation systems) and discuss the implications for AI reliability
Explore medical testing scenarios (sensitivity, specificity, false positives) as contexts for conditional probability, connecting the mathematics to real decision-making
Investigate how conditional probability applies to legal reasoning (e.g. prosecutor's fallacy) and discuss how misinterpretation of conditional language leads to incorrect conclusions
elaborations: using two-way tables and Venn diagrams to understand conditional statements and identify common mistakes in interpreting conditional language
using arrays and tree diagrams to represent, interpret and compare probabilities of dependent and independent events
investigating how conditional probability is used in natural language processing tasks (text/image generation, translation, recommendation systems)

AC9M10P02.minimum_width: Design and conduct a digital simulation of a conditional probability situation; interpret the simulated frequencies and compare them to theoretical probabilities.
AC9M10P02.typical_width: Design and conduct repeated simulations using digital tools for at least two conditional probability contexts; investigate sampling with and without replacement and identify when the difference becomes negligible; model counter-intuitive probability situations (e.g. Monty Hall, birthday problem); identify real-world uses of probability simulation (insurance, queueing, supply).
wider: Use simulation to model disease spread scenarios (e.g. flu infection rates) and discuss the ethical considerations of reporting probabilistic predictions to the public
Investigate how probability simulations are used in Monte Carlo methods for decision-making under uncertainty in finance or engineering contexts
Compare theoretical and simulated probabilities for increasingly complex dependent event scenarios, investigating how sample size affects the reliability of simulated estimates
elaborations: using samples of different sizes with and without replacement to identify when the difference becomes negligible
recognising that an event can be dependent on another event and how this affects probability calculation
using simulations for counter-intuitive situations (three-door problem, birthday problem)
identifying real-life situations where probability simulations are used (supply/demand, insurance risk, queueing)
using simulation to predict infection rates for a strain of flu or virus

AC9M10SP01.minimum_width: Construct a deductive proof for one geometric result (e.g. congruent triangles, angle property) using a sequence of logically connected statements; distinguish this proof from a practical demonstration.
AC9M10SP01.typical_width: Apply deductive reasoning to construct proofs involving congruent triangles, angle properties and similarity; deduce properties of geometric figures from established relationships; use theorems to solve multi-step spatial problems; distinguish proof from demonstration; investigate at least one visual proof.
wider: Investigate how automated theorem provers (ATP) and interactive proof assistants (IPA) allow mathematicians and AI systems to construct and verify formal proofs collaboratively
Use dynamic geometry software to investigate and prove properties of more complex configurations (e.g. shortest path in a rectangle, properties of cyclic quadrilaterals)
Explore the history of geometric proof from Euclid through to contemporary formal verification, examining how the standards of mathematical proof have evolved
elaborations: distinguishing between a practical demonstration and a proof
developing proofs involving congruent triangles and angle properties using logically connected statements
applying relationships to deduce properties of geometric figures (e.g. base angles of isosceles triangle)
investigating proofs of geometric theorems and applying logical reasoning and similarity to numerical exercises
using dynamic geometric software to investigate shortest paths and proving path properties
investigating how automated theorem provers (ATP) and interactive proof assistants (IPA) allow collaborative proof construction

AC9M10SP02.minimum_width: Interpret a network diagram representing a practical situation; identify nodes and edges and describe what connectedness means in that context.
AC9M10SP02.typical_width: Interpret networks and network diagrams across multiple practical situations (transport, social networks, electrical, ecological, mathematical); identify nodes and edges and explain what they represent; describe connectedness; demonstrate Euler's formula for polyhedra represented as networks; analyse at least one classical network problem (e.g. Königsberg bridges).
wider: Represent First Nations Australians' kinship systems using network diagrams and explore the significance of the relationships to Country/Place that the networks encode
Investigate how social networks, LANs or home wiring networks can be represented as network diagrams to identify practical problems (e.g. power overload, router placement)
Explore how metabolic networks, food webs or other biological/chemical structures are modelled as graphs and what network properties reveal about the system
elaborations: investigating how networks model authentic situations; recognising what nodes and edges represent
investigating network graphs analysing connectedness (e.g. Seven Bridges of Königsberg)
investigating how polyhedra can be represented as a network; demonstrating Euler's formula F+V=E+2
investigating how social networks, LANs, electrical wiring can be represented as network diagrams
investigating networks for travel, food webs, metabolic networks and other structures
representing First Nations Australians' kinship systems using network diagrams and exploring significance

AC9M10SP03.minimum_width: Design an algorithm (using pseudocode or flowchart) to solve a defined spatial problem; test the algorithm against at least two cases and identify any refinements needed.
AC9M10SP03.typical_width: Design, test and refine algorithms to solve spatial problems across at least two different contexts (scale models, floor plans, network routing, self-similar patterns); use digital tools to implement and validate; communicate and justify solutions in terms of the original problem; decompose complex spatial problems before algorithmic design.
wider: Explore geospatial technologies used by First Nations Australians' communities to address spatial problems including position and transformation, comparing these approaches to computational methods
Apply computational thinking to weighted network problems (e.g. shortest route, minimum spanning tree) and evaluate algorithm efficiency across different network sizes
Design algorithms for producing self-similar (fractal) patterns using recursion, validate with test cases and investigate the mathematical properties of the resulting patterns
elaborations: designing and making scale models of 3D objects using digital tools (e.g. 3D printing, tessellation-based puzzles)
applying computational thinking to network problems (connectedness, coverage, weighted measures)
defining and decomposing spatial problems; creating and applying algorithms; evaluating solutions
designing, creating and testing algorithms using pseudocode or flowcharts for self-similar patterns; validating using a range of test cases
exploring geospatial technologies used by First Nations Australians' communities

AC9M10ST01.minimum_width: Identify at least one specific misleading feature in a statistical report or graph (e.g. broken axis, non-representative sample) and explain how it affects the claim being made.
AC9M10ST01.typical_width: Analyse statistical claims, inferences and conclusions across multiple media contexts; identify misleading representations, unrepresentative samples, data not related to claims, and deliberate bias; investigate source and size of samples; discuss ethical considerations in reporting statistical data; distinguish valid from invalid statistical inferences.
wider: Use the concept of Indigenous data sovereignty to critique and evaluate the Australian Government's 'Closing the Gap' report, examining whose data is collected, how it is framed, and what claims are made
Investigate how identification of bias is a critical aspect of machine learning and deep learning, including how biased training data produces unfair or inaccurate AI systems

Analyse a specific case of statistical reporting in public health (e.g. infection rates, side effects) and evaluate the ethical responsibilities of researchers, media, and government in communicating probabilistic information
elaborations: identifying potentially misleading representations (broken axes, nonlinear scales); recognising when data is not representative or deliberately misleading
investigating source and size of sample; deciding whether representative of population
investigating population rates and ethical considerations when presenting infection rate data
using secondary data to predict infection/side effect rates; discussing ethical considerations of reporting
recognising how bias identification is critical in machine learning and deep learning
using Indigenous data sovereignty to critique the 'Closing the Gap' report

AC9M10ST02.minimum_width: Construct a boxplot from a data set; use it to describe the distribution in terms of centre, spread and any outliers in context.
AC9M10ST02.typical_width: Construct and interpret boxplots; compare two or more distributions using boxplots and other displays (histograms, dot plots, cumulative frequency graphs); calculate five-number summaries; describe shape (symmetry, skew, modality) in context; use digital tools to compare displays of the same data; discuss what different displays reveal and conceal.
wider: Investigate how outlier identification and handling is an important step in machine learning to prevent undue influence on models, and discuss criteria for deciding when to exclude outliers
Compare boxplots and histograms for the same real dataset to evaluate which display best addresses a specific statistical question, justifying the choice

Explore how the same distributional features (skew, outliers, spread) appear across multiple real contexts (biological, social, financial) and discuss what the shape of a distribution reveals about the underlying process
elaborations: constructing and interpreting box plots; using them to compare data sets
comparing shapes using box plots, histograms, cumulative frequency graphs and dot plots; discussing symmetry, skew and modality
using digital tools to compare boxplots and histograms for the same data
finding the five-number summary and using its graphical representation to compare centre and spread
comparing information from different displays
exploring how identification and handling of outliers is important in machine learning

AC9M10ST03.minimum_width: Construct a scatterplot for a bivariate data set; describe the association in terms of strength and direction (positive/negative/no association).
AC9M10ST03.typical_width: Construct scatterplots and comment on association (strength, direction, linearity) across multiple data contexts; distinguish association from causation; use a line of good fit by eye to discuss reliability of predictions; make, justify and critique claims about association using statistical evidence.
wider: Investigate the relationship between 2 variables of spear throwers used by First Peoples of Australia using real data; construct scatterplots, make comparisons and draw conclusions

Investigate AI systems that analyse bivariate data to forecast or make predictions using correlation analysis; discuss limitations including inability to capture causality or account for ethical implications
Explore how scatter plots and correlation are used in data science for feature engineering and model assessment in machine learning, and discuss what correlation analysis can and cannot tell us
elaborations: discussing the difference between association and cause and effect in contexts such as health, diversity and climate
using statistical evidence to make, justify and critique claims about association (climate change, migration, social media)
informally using a line of good fit by eye to discuss reliability of predictions
exploring how scatter plots help data scientists gain insights and can be applied to machine learning
investigating AI systems that analyse bivariate data to forecast; discussing limitations
investigating the relationship between 2 variables of spear throwers used by First Peoples of Australia

AC9M10ST04.minimum_width: Construct a two-way table from a categorical data set; identify at least one pattern or possible relationship between the two variables.
AC9M10ST04.typical_width: Construct two-way tables for categorical data in multiple contexts; use percentages and proportions to identify patterns and associations; compare response patterns across categories (e.g. Likert scales across year groups); discuss whether observed patterns suggest a relationship; acknowledge limitations of two-way table analysis.
wider: Conduct a real school investigation (e.g. litter survey) collecting and analysing two categorical variables, writing a report that discusses whether the pattern found suggests a genuine relationship

Investigate how two-way tables are used in medical research or public health (e.g. treatment vs outcome, exposure vs disease) and discuss the difference between association and causation in these contexts
Explore how two-way frequency tables connect to conditional probability, linking the work of AC9M10P01 to the statistical investigation context
elaborations: using two-way tables to investigate Likert scale survey responses across two categories of respondents
recording data in two-way tables; using percentages and proportions to identify patterns and associations
conducting a litter survey considering relationships between categorical variables (day of week, weather)

AC9M10ST05.minimum_width: Plan and conduct a statistical investigation involving bivariate data; collect, display and describe the data; identify at least one limitation of any inference drawn.
AC9M10ST05.typical_width: Plan and conduct statistical investigations involving bivariate data through observation, experiment or measurement; graph, interpret and analyse data; report findings including discussion of association, limitations of interpolation/extrapolation, data validity, and appropriate strength-of-evidence language.
wider: Investigate biodiversity changes in Australia before and after colonisation by comparing relevant bivariate data sets; discuss and report on associations with consideration of data provenance and historical context

Conduct a statistical investigation addressing a real anecdotal claim (e.g. about climate, housing, natural resources) evaluating data validity, inference limitations and communicating findings to a specified audience

Investigate the statistical question 'Is there a relationship between vaccination rates and immunity outcomes?' using secondary data; report findings with explicit discussion of limitations and ethical considerations
elaborations: designing investigations collecting bivariate data through observation, experiment or measurement; graphing, interpreting and reporting in context
investigating anecdotal claims (climate, housing, natural resources) with consideration of data validity and limitations of interpolation/extrapolation
using statistical investigation to address the question about vaccines and immunity
investigating biodiversity changes before and after colonisation by comparing bivariate data; reporting on associations
